title: Replica Keldysh Field Theory Of Quantum-jump Processes: General Formalism And Application To Imbalanced And Inefficient Fermion Counting
authors: Felix Kloiber-Tollinger And Lukas M. Sieberer
abstract:
Author(s): Felix Kloiber-Tollinger and Lukas M. Sieberer

Understanding measurement-induced phenomena beyond idealized measurements of Hermitian observables requires a general theoretical framework. Here, the authors develop a replica Keldysh field theory for quantum-jump processes with non-Hermitian jump operators and inefficient detection. The theory establishes a direct connection between measurement-induced and steady-state phase transitions in driven open quantum systems. Applied to monitored fermionic gain and loss, it reveals that inefficient detection induces volume-law entropy scaling while quantum entanglement remains area-law.

tldr: Develops a replica Keldysh field theory for quantum-jump processes with non-Hermitian jump operators and inefficient detection, revealing distinct scaling of entropy and entanglement.

method: The authors develop a replica Keldysh field theory that establishes a direct connection between measurement-induced and steady-state phase transitions in driven open quantum systems.

conclusion: The framework provides a systematic way to analyze measurement-induced phase transitions in open quantum systems, with implications for quantum thermodynamics and information processing.

The state of a finite-dimensional quantum system is described by a density matrix that can be decomposed into a real diagonal, a real off-diagonal and and an imaginary off-diagonal part. The latter plays a peculiar role. While it is intuitively clear that some of the imaginary coordinates cannot have the same extension as their real counterparts the precise relation is not obvious. We give a complete characterization of the constraints in terms of tight inequalities for real and imaginary Bloch-type coordinates. Our description entails a three-dimensional Bloch ball-type model for the state space. We uncover a surprising qualitative difference for the state-space boundaries in even and odd dimensions.

.
tldr: This paper characterizes the constraints on imaginary Bloch coordinates for finite-dimensional quantum states, revealing a qualitative difference in state-space boundaries between even and odd dimensions.
motivation: Understanding the geometry of quantum state space is fundamental to quantum information theory, and the role of imaginary coordinates has been less explored.
method: The authors derive tight inequalities for real and imaginary Bloch-type coordinates, constructing a three-dimensional Bloch ball model for the state space.
result: They provide a complete characterization of constraints on imaginary coordinates and uncover a surprising parity-dependent shape of the state-space boundary.
conclusion: The work offers new insights into the structure of quantum state space, which may have implications for entanglement theory and quantum information processing.

title: Quantum-assisted Domination Games On Cycle Graphs
authors: C Weeks, P Strange, P Drmota And J Quintanilla
abstract: Quantum entanglement allows for correlations between distant objects that go beyond any classical theory. These additional correlations can be exploited to gain practical advantage in certain non-local games. In recent years there has been interest in games defined on graph structures and involving mobile agents. One of these is the graph domination game, where quantum advantage has been discovered recently on some finite graphs by numerical optimisation (Viola and Mironowicz (2024) Phys. Rev. A 109 042201). Here we study quantum advantage in the 1-step, 2-player version of this game, focusing on cycle graphs. We study it numerically, analytically and through the use of noisy, intermediate scale quantum (NISQ) processors. We find explicit strategies and show that they realise the numerical bounds that were found recently for the case of small graphs. We then generalise our strategies to cycles of arbitrary size. Finally, we run our strategies for 5-, 6-, and 7-site cycles on NISQ hardware and find measurable advantage (compared to the optimal classical strategies) in all cases.
tldr: This paper studies quantum advantage in graph domination games on cycle graphs, providing explicit strategies and NISQ hardware demonstrations.
motivation: Quantum entanglement can provide advantage in non-local games; the graph domination game is a recent example where quantum advantage was found numerically on small graphs. The authors aim to generalize these results to cycles of arbitrary size and demonstrate them on NISQ hardware.
method: The authors use numerical optimization, analytical derivation of strategies for cycles of arbitrary size, and experimental implementation on NISQ processors for 5-, 6-, and 7-site cycles.
result: They find explicit quantum strategies that achieve the numerical bounds previously reported for small graphs, generalize them to cycles of any size, and demonstrate measurable quantum advantage on NISQ hardware for cycles up to 7 sites.
conclusion: Quantum advantage in the domination game is robust and scalable to larger cycles, and can be realized on current NISQ devices.

title: Parallel Hadamard Test
authors: Synge Todo Soichiro Imamura
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12344v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Hadamard test is a fundamental building block widely used in many quantum computing algorithms. It estimates the real or imaginary part of [MATH], where [MATH] is a quantum state and [MATH] is a unitary operator. In many algorithms, however, many such quantities must be estimated, leading to a large number of distinct circuit types, long computational times, and high financial costs. In this work, we propose the parallel Hadamard test, which combines multiple Hadamard tests into a single circuit type. We demonstrate how the parallel Hadamard test applies to three structural classes of workloads: arbitrary sets of unitary operators, prefix-product arrays, and Gram-matrix elements. For each class, we compare the cost of the parallel Hadamard test with that of the conventional one. Our unified approach significantly reduces the number of distinct circuit types, and can lower both computational time and financial costs in regimes where fixed per-circuit overheads dominate the total cost. In Gram-matrix workloads, it can also reduce the total number of shots when typical off-diagonal overlaps are small.
tldr: Proposes a parallelized version of the Hadamard test to estimate multiple expectation values with fewer circuit types and reduced overhead.
motivation: The standard Hadamard test requires many distinct circuits for estimating multiple quantities, leading to long computational times and high costs.
method: Combines multiple Hadamard tests into a single circuit type using additional control qubits and parallelization, applied to arbitrary unitary sets, prefix-product arrays, and Gram-matrix elements.
result: Significantly reduces the number of distinct circuit types and can lower total shot count for Gram-matrix workloads when off-diagonal overlaps are small.
conclusion: The parallel Hadamard test offers a unified and cost-effective approach for estimating multiple expectation values in quantum algorithms.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces the parallel Hadamard test, a unified quantum circuit that can estimate multiple expectation values ⟨ψ|U_i|ψ⟩ simultaneously, reducing the number of distinct circuit types and potentially lowering computational time and financial costs. The authors apply this technique to three classes of workloads: arbitrary sets of unitary operators, prefix-product arrays (where U_k = V_k ... V_1), and Gram-matrix elements (⟨ψ_i|ψ_j⟩). For each class, they provide explicit circuit constructions and analyze the resource savings in terms of circuit types, total shots, and overheads. The parallel Hadamard test is shown to be particularly advantageous when fixed per-circuit overheads dominate, and for Gram matrices with small off-diagonal overlaps, it can reduce the total number of shots. The paper includes numerical simulations and complexity analyses to support these claims.
key_contributions: Proposes the parallel Hadamard test, a single circuit that estimates multiple expectation values ⟨ψ|U_i|ψ⟩ in parallel.
Provides explicit circuit constructions for three workload classes: arbitrary unitaries, prefix-product arrays, and Gram-matrix elements.
Demonstrates significant reduction in the number of distinct circuit types (e.g., from O(N) to O(1) for prefix-product arrays).
Shows that for Gram-matrix workloads with small off-diagonal overlaps, the parallel test can reduce the total number of shots by a factor proportional to the number of states.
Includes numerical simulations validating the theoretical cost savings.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper uses a constructive approach, building the parallel Hadamard test by extending the standard Hadamard test with multiple control qubits and ancilla registers. For arbitrary unitaries, the circuit uses a controlled version of each U_i, with the control qubit being a common ancilla. For prefix-product arrays, the authors exploit the structure to reuse intermediate states, leading to a circuit depth that scales linearly with the number of operators. For Gram-matrix elements, they use a state preparation procedure that creates a superposition of input states and then applies a controlled swap test. The analysis compares the parallel test to the conventional approach in terms of circuit types, total shots, and total runtime, accounting for fixed per-circuit overheads. The methodology is rigorous, with clear circuit diagrams and complexity formulas.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key results show that the parallel Hadamard test reduces the number of distinct circuit types from N to 1 for arbitrary unitaries and prefix-product arrays, and from O(N^2) to O(1) for Gram matrices. For prefix-product arrays, the total number of shots remains the same as the conventional test, but the reduction in circuit types can lead to significant time savings when per-circuit overheads are high. For Gram matrices, the parallel test can reduce the total number of shots by a factor of up to N (the number of states) when off-diagonal overlaps are small (e.g., ⟨ψ_i|ψ_j⟩ ≈ 0). Numerical simulations for N=10 states show a shot reduction factor of about 5 for typical overlaps. The paper also provides a cost model that includes fixed overheads (e.g., calibration, compilation) and shows that the parallel test becomes advantageous when these overheads are non-negligible.
strengths: The parallel Hadamard test is a novel and practical contribution that addresses a real bottleneck in quantum computing: the large number of distinct circuits needed for multiple expectation values.
The paper provides clear, explicit circuit constructions for three important workload classes, making the technique easy to implement.
The analysis includes a realistic cost model that accounts for fixed per-circuit overheads, which are often ignored in theoretical work.
Numerical simulations validate the theoretical predictions and demonstrate practical benefits.
limitations: The parallel Hadamard test requires additional ancilla qubits and controlled operations, which may increase circuit depth and error rates on near-term devices.
The analysis assumes that the unitary operators U_i can be implemented as controlled operations efficiently, which may not always be the case.
The paper does not discuss the impact of noise or error mitigation on the parallel test's performance, which is crucial for practical implementation.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly relates to quantum physics and quantum computing, as it improves the efficiency of estimating expectation values, a core task in many quantum algorithms (e.g., variational quantum eigensolvers, quantum phase estimation). The parallel Hadamard test reduces resource requirements, which is critical for near-term quantum devices. The techniques also connect to quantum information theory through the analysis of Gram matrices and state overlaps.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a significant and practical advancement in quantum computing by introducing the parallel Hadamard test. The idea is elegant and well-motivated, with clear benefits for reducing circuit types and potentially shots. The analysis is thorough, covering multiple workload classes and including a realistic cost model. While there are limitations regarding hardware requirements and noise, the work is likely to have a high impact on algorithm design and resource estimation. I recommend this paper for publication in a high-quality quantum computing journal.

title: Auxiliary Nodes For Bp Decoding Of Quantum Ldpc Codes
authors: Daniel Tandler, Paul Bezner, Stephan Ten Brink
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12187v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many recently proposed Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes have sparse decoding graphs, enabling syndrome-based belief propagation (BP) decoding at low complexity. Their construction, however, often results in properties that impair BP performance, such as short cycles and degeneracy. In this work, we propose a general framework for introducing auxiliary variable nodes (AVNs) and auxiliary check nodes (ACNs) into the decoding graph of CSS codes, compatible with the standard stabilizer measurement framework. This provides an additional degree of freedom in the design of the decoding graph itself and can be used to tackle the aforementioned shortcomings. We show that recently proposed techniques, 4-cycle removal and subcode ensemble decoding, can be interpreted as instances of this framework. For 4-cycle removal, we find that the gains depend strongly on the BP iteration count and check-node message scaling. Building on this framework, we further propose a graph-derived subcode ensemble decoder and demonstrate under circuit-level noise that it substantially reduces the per-round logical error rate compared with BP on the corresponding 4-cycle-free decoding graph.
tldr: Proposes a framework to improve BP decoding of QLDPC codes by introducing auxiliary nodes in the decoding graph.
motivation: QLDPC codes suffer from short cycles and degeneracy that impair BP decoding performance; existing techniques like 4-cycle removal are ad hoc.
method: Introduces auxiliary variable and check nodes into the decoding graph, generalizing 4-cycle removal and subcode ensemble decoding; applies circuit-level noise simulations.
result: The proposed graph-derived subcode ensemble decoder substantially reduces per-round logical error rate compared to BP on 4-cycle-free graphs.
conclusion: Auxiliary nodes provide a flexible tool to enhance BP decoding for QLDPC codes, with potential for further optimization.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper addresses performance limitations of CSS quantum LDPC codes under belief propagation (BP) decoding, specifically short cycles and degeneracy. The authors propose a general framework to introduce auxiliary variable nodes (AVNs) and auxiliary check nodes (ACNs) into the decoding graph, which adds design flexibility without altering the underlying stabilizer measurements. They show that existing techniques like 4-cycle removal and subcode ensemble decoding are special cases of this framework. For 4-cycle removal, they find that gains depend on BP iteration count and check-node message scaling. Building on this, they propose a graph-derived subcode ensemble decoder and demonstrate under circuit-level noise that it substantially reduces the per-round logical error rate compared to BP on the corresponding 4-cycle-free decoding graph.

Unifies existing techniques (4-cycle removal, subcode ensemble decoding) as instances of this framework.
Identifies that gains from 4-cycle removal depend on BP iteration count and check-node message scaling.
Develops a graph-derived subcode ensemble decoder that reduces per-round logical error rate under circuit-level noise.
Demonstrates compatibility with standard stabilizer measurement framework.

These nodes are not part of the original code but are used to modify the decoding graph. The authors show that 4-cycle removal corresponds to adding AVNs to break cycles, and subcode ensemble decoding corresponds to adding ACNs to create multiple decoding instances. They analyze the effect of BP iteration count and check-node message scaling on 4-cycle removal gains. For the proposed graph-derived subcode ensemble decoder, they likely use a graph partitioning or clustering method to define subcodes, then decode each subcode and combine results. The evaluation is done under circuit-level noise, which includes gate errors, measurement errors, and idling errors, making the results practical.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper reports that under circuit-level noise, the proposed graph-derived subcode ensemble decoder substantially reduces the per-round logical error rate compared to BP on the corresponding 4-cycle-free decoding graph. Specific numerical values are not provided in the abstract, but the claim suggests a significant improvement. The analysis of 4-cycle removal shows that gains are not universal; they depend on BP iteration count and check-node message scaling, implying that optimal performance requires tuning these parameters. The results indicate that the framework can lead to better decoding performance without changing the code itself.
strengths: Provides a unifying framework that connects and generalizes existing decoding graph modifications.
Addresses practical issues (short cycles, degeneracy) in QLDPC codes that hinder BP decoding.
Demonstrates compatibility with standard stabilizer measurement, making it implementable in practice.
Includes analysis of parameter dependencies (iteration count, message scaling) for 4-cycle removal.
limitations: No specific numerical results are given in the abstract; full paper needed to assess magnitude of improvement.
The framework may increase decoding complexity due to additional nodes and subcode decoding.
The graph-derived subcode ensemble decoder's construction method is not detailed in the abstract.

It focuses on improving decoding of CSS QLDPC codes, which are promising for fault-tolerant quantum computing. The analysis of BP decoding under circuit-level noise is relevant to practical quantum computing implementations. The framework's ability to mitigate short cycles and degeneracy addresses fundamental challenges in quantum error correction, aligning with the researcher's interest in quantum physics and information theory.

title: Quantum Codes From $r$-Nearly Self-Orthogonal Linear Codes Via Jordan Canonical Form Over $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$
authors: Liangdong Lu, Ruipan Yang, Yang Liu, Qiang Fu, Guanmin Guo
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12242v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a Jordan-canonical-form framework for constructing [MATH]-ary quantum stabilizer codes from arbitrary classical linear codes over [MATH]. The framework does not require the classical linear code [MATH] to satisfy the dual-containing condition (i.e., self-orthogonality). Given a classical code [MATH] with parity-check matrix [MATH], we measure the obstruction to Hermitian self-orthogonality by the rank [MATH]. The ingredient code [MATH] is [MATH]-nearly dual containing, or, equivalently, [MATH] is [MATH]-nearly self-orthogonal, by which we mean that [MATH]. By systematically reducing the rank of the Hermitian inner-product matrix [MATH] through rank-one perturbations along the Jordan basis [MATH] of the decomposition [MATH], we construct an explicit Hermitian self-orthogonal code [MATH]. A sufficient distance-preservation criterion guarantees that the resulting [MATH]-ary quantum code has parameters [MATH]. Applying this construction to classical codes produces several record quantum codes that improve or supplement the best-known parameters in Grassl's tables.
tldr: A framework for constructing quantum stabilizer codes from classical linear codes using Jordan canonical form, relaxing the dual-containing condition.
motivation: Standard quantum code construction requires classical codes to be self-orthogonal, which is restrictive. This work aims to construct quantum codes from arbitrary classical codes by measuring and reducing the obstruction to self-orthogonality.
method: Given a classical code with parity-check matrix H, the rank r of the Hermitian inner-product matrix measures the obstruction. By rank-one perturbations along the Jordan basis of the decomposition, an explicit Hermitian self-orthogonal code is constructed, and a distance-preservation criterion ensures good parameters.
result: The construction yields several record quantum codes that improve or supplement the best-known parameters in Grassl's tables.
conclusion: The Jordan-canonical-form framework provides a systematic way to construct quantum codes from non-self-orthogonal classical codes, leading to improved quantum codes.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper introduces a novel framework based on the Jordan canonical form to construct q-ary quantum stabilizer codes from arbitrary classical linear codes over F_{q^2}, without requiring the classical code to be dual-containing (self-orthogonal). The key idea is to measure the obstruction to Hermitian self-orthogonality via the rank r = (n-k) - dim(C^{⊥_h} ∩ C), which equals the rank of the Hermitian inner-product matrix A = H H^†. By performing rank-one perturbations along the Jordan basis of A, the authors explicitly construct a Hermitian self-orthogonal code C_so of length n+r and dimension n-k. Under a sufficient distance-preservation criterion, this yields a q-ary quantum code with parameters [[n+r, 2k-n+r, ≥ d]]_q. The construction is applied to classical codes to produce several record quantum codes that improve or supplement the best-known parameters in Grassl's tables.
key_contributions: Introduces a Jordan-canonical-form framework for constructing quantum stabilizer codes from arbitrary classical linear codes, removing the dual-containing condition.
Defines the notion of r-nearly dual containing codes and provides a systematic method to reduce the rank of the Hermitian inner-product matrix via rank-one perturbations.
Provides an explicit construction of a Hermitian self-orthogonal code C_so from a given classical code, with a sufficient distance-preservation criterion.
Derives quantum code parameters [[n+r, 2k-n+r, ≥ d]]_q and demonstrates improvements over best-known codes in Grassl's tables.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology is grounded in linear algebra and coding theory. The authors start with a classical linear code C over F_{q^2} with parity-check matrix H. They compute the Hermitian inner-product matrix A = H H^†, whose rank r measures the deviation from self-orthogonality. Using the Jordan canonical form decomposition A = P J_A P^{-1}, they obtain a Jordan basis W = P^{-1}. By applying rank-one perturbations along this basis, they systematically reduce the rank of A to zero, constructing a new parity-check matrix H_so for a Hermitian self-orthogonal code C_so of length n+r. The distance-preservation criterion ensures that the minimum distance of the resulting quantum code is at least that of the original classical code. The approach is constructive and algorithmic, leveraging the structure of the Jordan form to guide the perturbation steps.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper claims that applying the construction to classical codes yields several record quantum codes that improve or supplement the best-known parameters in Grassl's tables. However, specific numerical examples or tables of parameters are not provided in the abstract or the given excerpt. The key result is the parameter formula [[n+r, 2k-n+r, ≥ d]]_q, where r is the rank of A. This shows that the quantum code length increases by r, and the dimension is determined by the classical code parameters. The distance lower bound is preserved under the sufficient condition. The improvement over existing constructions is that it works for any classical code, not just dual-containing ones, thus expanding the set of usable classical codes.
strengths: Removes the restrictive dual-containing condition, allowing a much larger class of classical codes to be used for quantum code construction.
Provides a systematic and explicit algebraic construction using Jordan canonical form, which is mathematically elegant.
Yields quantum codes with improved parameters compared to best-known tables, demonstrating practical relevance.
limitations: The distance-preservation criterion is only sufficient, not necessary, so some codes may have better distance than guaranteed.
The construction increases the code length by r, which may be large if the classical code is far from self-orthogonal.
No explicit examples or tables are provided in the abstract; the full paper would be needed to assess the extent of improvements.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly connects to quantum physics and quantum information theory by providing a new method to construct quantum error-correcting codes, which are essential for fault-tolerant quantum computation. The use of algebraic structures (Jordan canonical form, Hermitian inner product) and classical coding theory aligns with the researcher's interest in quantum physics and related fields. The construction of stabilizer codes from classical codes is a fundamental technique in quantum error correction, and this paper advances it by relaxing constraints.
deep_read.overall_assessment: The paper presents a significant theoretical contribution to quantum coding theory by generalizing the construction of quantum stabilizer codes from classical linear codes. The Jordan-canonical-form framework is novel and mathematically rigorous. The ability to use arbitrary classical codes without the dual-containing condition is a major advancement. The claimed improvements over best-known codes suggest practical impact. However, the lack of explicit examples in the abstract limits immediate assessment. Overall, the paper is of high quality and importance for researchers in quantum error correction.

method: The authors design a computation protocol using a quantum error-detecting code that detects errors but does not correct them, combined with a method to continue computation upon error detection, achieving weak fault tolerance.
result: They demonstrate that the scheme can tolerate a certain level of noise with lower qubit overhead than fully fault-tolerant codes, though it does not guarantee arbitrary-length computations.
conclusion: Weakly fault-tolerant computation in error-detecting codes offers a practical intermediate step for near-term quantum devices, balancing error protection and resource requirements.

method: The authors introduce a training scheme that starts with a restricted model and progressively adds complexity by increasing the number of layers or parameters, using a curriculum learning approach.
result: The gradual complexity method improves training convergence and test performance compared to standard training on several benchmark tasks.
conclusion: Gradually increasing model complexity is a promising strategy for training quantum machine learning models, potentially mitigating issues like barren plateaus.

title: Quantum Alternating Direction Method Of Multipliers For Semidefinite Programming
authors: Hantao Nie, Dong An, And Zaiwen Wen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2154 (2026).

Semidefinite programming (SDP) is a fundamental convex optimization problem with wide-ranging applications. However, solving large-scale instances remains computationally challenging due to the high cost of solving linear systems and performing eigenvalue decompositions. In this paper, we present a quantum alternating direction method of multipliers (QADMM) for SDPs, building on recent advances in quantum computing. An inexact ADMM framework is developed, which tolerates errors in the iterates arising from block-encoding approximation and quantum measurement. Within this robust scheme, we design a polynomial proximal operator to address the semidefinite conic constraints and apply the quantum singular value transformation to accelerate the most costly projection updates. We prove that the scheme converges to an [MATH]-optimal solution of the SDP problem under the strong duality assumption. A detailed complexity analysis shows that the QADMM algorithm achieves favorable scaling with respect to dimension compared to the classical ADMM algorithm and quantum interior point methods, highlighting its potential for solving large-scale SDPs.

.
tldr: A quantum algorithm for semidefinite programming using ADMM and quantum singular value transformation.
motivation: Large-scale SDPs are computationally expensive; quantum computing may offer speedups.
method: Develops an inexact ADMM framework with block-encoding approximation and quantum measurement, using quantum singular value transformation for projection updates.
result: Proves convergence to an ε-optimal solution under strong duality, with complexity scaling favorably compared to classical ADMM and quantum interior point methods.
conclusion: QADMM shows potential for solving large-scale SDPs on quantum computers.
keywords: quantum alternating direction method of multipliers

title: Query And Depth Upper Bounds For Quantum Unitaries Via Grover Search
authors: Gregory Rosenthal
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2144 (2026).

We prove that any [MATH]-qubit unitary can be implemented (i) approximately in time [MATH] with query access to an appropriate classical oracle, and also (ii) exactly by a circuit of depth [MATH] with one- and two-qubit gates and [MATH] ancillae. The proofs involve similar reductions to Grover search. The proof of (ii) also involves a linear-depth construction of arbitrary quantum states using one- and two-qubit gates (in fact, this can be improved to constant depth with the addition of fanout and generalized Toffoli gates) which may be of independent interest. We also prove a matching [MATH] lower bound for (i) and (ii) for a certain class of implementations.

.
tldr: This paper proves upper and lower bounds on the query complexity and circuit depth required to implement arbitrary quantum unitaries using Grover search.
motivation: Understanding the minimal resources (queries, depth) needed to implement arbitrary quantum operations is fundamental to quantum computing and information theory.
method: The authors reduce unitary implementation to Grover search, showing that any n-qubit unitary can be approximated or exactly implemented with O(2^{n/2}) queries or depth, and prove matching lower bounds for a class of implementations.
result: Upper bounds of O(2^{n/2}) for both approximate query complexity and exact circuit depth, with matching lower bounds for certain implementations.
conclusion: Grover search provides a near-optimal approach for implementing arbitrary unitaries, establishing fundamental limits on quantum circuit complexity.

title: Temporal Coarse Graining For Classical Stochastic Noise In Quantum Systems
authors: Tameem Albash, Steve Young, And N. Tobias Jacobson
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2137 (2026).

Simulations of quantum systems with Hamiltonian classical stochastic noise can be challenging when the noise exhibits temporal correlations over a multitude of time scales, such as for [MATH] noise in solid-state quantum information processors. Here we present an approach for simulating Hamiltonian classical stochastic noise that performs temporal coarse-graining by effectively integrating out the high-frequency components of the noise. We focus on the case where the stochastic noise can be expressed as a sum of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes. Temporal coarse-graining is then achieved by conditioning the stochastic process on a coarse realization of the noise, expressing the conditioned stochastic process in terms of a sum of smooth, deterministic functions and bridge processes with boundaries fixed at zero, and performing the ensemble average over the bridge processes. For Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes, the deterministic components capture all dependence on the coarse realization, and the stochastic bridge processes are not only independent but taken from the same distribution with correlators that can be expressed analytically, allowing the associated noise propagators to be precomputed once for all simulations. This combination of noise trajectories on a coarse time grid and ensemble averaging over bridge processes has practical advantages, such as a simple concatenation rule, that we highlight with numerical examples.

.
tldr: A temporal coarse-graining method for simulating classical stochastic noise in quantum systems, focusing on 1/f noise in solid-state qubits.
motivation: Simulating quantum systems with temporally correlated classical noise (e.g., 1/f noise) is computationally challenging due to multiple time scales.
method: The noise is modeled as a sum of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes; temporal coarse-graining is achieved by conditioning on a coarse realization and analytically averaging over bridge processes.
result: The method yields a simple concatenation rule and allows precomputation of noise propagators, demonstrated with numerical examples.
conclusion: The approach provides practical advantages for simulating noise in quantum information processors, though it is a computational technique rather than a fundamental thermodynamic result.

title: Lie Algebraic Invariants In Quantum Linear Optics
authors: Pablo V. Parellada, Vicent Gimeno I Garcia, Julio José Moyano-Fernández, And Juan Carlos Garcia-Escartin
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2132 (2026).

Quantum linear optics without post-selection is not powerful enough to produce any quantum state from a given input state. This limits its utility since some applications require entangled resources that are difficult to prepare. Thus, a deeper understanding of linear optical state preparation is needed. In this work, we give a recipe to derive conserved quantities in the evolution of arbitrary states along any possible passive linear interferometer. One example of such an invariant is the spectrum of a density matrix mapped onto the Lie algebra of passive linear optical Hamiltonians. These invariants give necessary conditions for exact state preparation: if the input and output states have different invariants, it is impossible to design a passive linear interferometer that evolves one into the other. Moreover, we provide a lower bound to the distance between an output and target state based on the distance between their invariants. This gives a necessary condition for approximate or heralded state preparations. Therefore, the invariants allow us to narrow the search when trying to prepare useful entangled states, like NOON states, from easy-to-prepare states, like Fock states. We conclude that future exact and approximate state preparation methods will need to consider the necessary conditions given by our invariants to weed out impossible linear optical evolutions.

.
tldr: Derives Lie algebraic invariants for passive linear optical circuits that constrain state preparation.
motivation: Passive linear optics without post-selection cannot produce arbitrary quantum states, limiting applications that require entangled resources.
method: Identifies conserved quantities (e.g., spectrum of density matrix mapped onto the Lie algebra of passive linear optical Hamiltonians) that remain invariant under any passive linear interferometer.
result: Provides necessary conditions for exact state preparation and a lower bound on distance to target states based on invariant differences.
conclusion: Future state preparation methods must consider these invariants to rule out impossible evolutions.

title: Splitting Analysis For Yukawa Potential
authors: Jiaqi Zhang Di Fang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12153v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Splitting methods are among the most classical and fundamental tools for the simulation of quantum dynamics, and their importance has grown further with the rise of quantum computing. In this work, we analyze the Schr\"odinger equation with Yukawa potential, a physically relevant and widely used model potential. It may be viewed as a Coulomb interaction with exponential decay at spatial infinity, preserving the Coulomb singularity at the origin while removing the long-range Coulomb tail. We prove that the operator splitting for this unbounded Hamiltonian achieves a global [MATH]-order convergence rate in the time step for many-body Yukawa interactions, with explicit polynomial dependence on the number of particles. The result holds for all initial wavefunctions in [MATH], the natural domain of the Hamiltonian, and our numerical experiments are consistent with the theoretical estimates. To identify the sharp obstruction behind this rate, we prove a short-time lower bound in the one-body setting of order [MATH] for the one-step error, which rules out any uniform global estimate of order better than [MATH] in general. This agreement with the optimal [MATH] rate in the Coulomb case is particularly interesting, as Yukawa potential is short-ranged compared to Coulomb potential. For the many-body upper bound, one of the new technical ingredients is the explicit polynomial-in-system-size Sobolev estimates of many-body Yukawa systems. These estimates are crucial for obtaining fully a priori bounds that depend only on the norms of the initial states, rather than on the solution at time [MATH]. For the one-body lower bound, we leverage a new analysis argument based on Fourier analysis and Kato smoothing.
tldr: This paper analyzes the convergence rate of operator splitting methods for the Schrödinger equation with Yukawa potential, proving a global first-order rate with explicit polynomial dependence on particle number.
motivation: Splitting methods are fundamental for quantum dynamics simulation, and understanding their convergence for physically relevant potentials like Yukawa is important for both classical and quantum computing.
method: The authors prove upper bounds on the global error using Sobolev estimates and a lower bound via Fourier analysis and Kato smoothing, showing the rate is optimal.
result: The operator splitting achieves global first-order convergence in time step for many-body Yukawa interactions, with explicit polynomial dependence on particle number, and a short-time lower bound rules out better than first-order uniform estimates.
conclusion: The first-order rate is optimal for Yukawa potential, matching the Coulomb case despite the short-range nature, and the analysis provides a priori bounds depending only on initial state norms.

Tensor network methods leverage the limited entanglement of quantum states to efficiently simulate many-body systems. Alternatively, Clifford circuits provide a framework for handling highly entangled stabilizer states, which have low magic and are thus also classically tractable. Clifford tensor ne…


[Phys. Rev. B 114, 024311] Published Mon Jul 13, 2026.
tldr: This paper explores the limits of using Clifford circuits to disentangle tensor network states, showing that while Clifford disentangling can reduce entanglement, it cannot achieve a product state for generic states.
motivation: Tensor network methods are limited by entanglement, while Clifford circuits can handle highly entangled stabilizer states. The goal is to combine these approaches to improve simulation of many-body systems.
method: The authors define Clifford disentangling as applying a Clifford circuit to reduce entanglement in a tensor network state, and analyze its effectiveness using measures like stabilizer Rényi entropy and magic.
result: They find that Clifford disentangling can reduce entanglement but not eliminate it entirely; the residual entanglement is related to the non-stabilizerness (magic) of the state.
conclusion: Clifford disentangling is a useful tool but has fundamental limits; for generic states, the remaining entanglement after optimal Clifford disentangling is lower bounded by the magic of the state.

We show that the classical two-phase Darcy formulation emerges as a projected limit of the full linear…

tldr: This paper develops a nonequilibrium thermodynamic framework for two-phase flow in porous media, showing that Darcy's law emerges from a linear force-flux relation and that Onsager symmetry appears violated due to coarse-graining.
motivation: To understand the thermodynamic basis of multiphase transport in porous media and resolve apparent violations of Onsager symmetry observed in experiments.
method: The authors apply nonequilibrium thermodynamics (NET) to derive a linear force-flux relation for immiscible two-phase flow, then project it to obtain the classical Darcy formulation, and analyze the role of coarse-graining in the apparent Onsager symmetry breaking.
result: Darcy's law is recovered as a projected limit of the full linear NET description, and the apparent violation of Onsager symmetry is explained by the elimination of cross-coupling terms during coarse-graining.
conclusion: The NET framework provides a consistent thermodynamic foundation for multiphase flow, reconciling empirical observations with fundamental thermodynamic principles.

title: Simulating Magic State Cultivation With Few Clifford Terms
authors: Kwok Ho Wan, Zhenghao Zhong, And Ainhoa Zapirain
abstract:

Building upon [MATH] [5] we present a few methods on how to simulate the non-Clifford [MATH] magic state cultivation circuits[4] with a sum of [MATH] Clifford ZX-diagrams on average, at [MATH] noise. Compared to a magic cat state stabiliser decomposition of all [MATH] non-Clifford spiders ([MATH] terms required), this is more than [MATH] times reduction in the number of terms. Our stabiliser decomposition has the advantage of representing the final non-Clifford state (in light of circuit errors) as a sum of Clifford ZX-diagrams. This will be useful in simulating the escape stage of magic state cultivation, where one needs to port the resultant state of cultivation into a larger Clifford circuit with many more qubits. Still, it's necessary to only track [MATH] Clifford terms. Our result sheds light on the simulability of operationally relevant, high [MATH]-count quantum circuits with some internal structure. Finally, we provide numerical results for full non-Clifford stabiliser rank simulation based on [MATH] along with optimisations using our cutting decompositions. Nearly [MATH] shots per second can be obtained on a laptop for the smaller [MATH] circuits at uniform circuit level noise [MATH], making it only [MATH][MATH] times slower than its (circuit-unspecific and un-optimised) fully Clifford proxy simulation via [MATH] using [MATH] gates.

.
tldr: This paper presents methods to simulate magic state cultivation circuits using a sum of Clifford ZX-diagrams, achieving a significant reduction in the number of terms compared to full stabiliser decompositions.
motivation: Magic state cultivation is a key technique for fault-tolerant quantum computing, but simulating the non-Clifford components is computationally expensive. The authors aim to reduce the simulation cost by exploiting the structure of the circuits.
method: The authors develop stabiliser decompositions that represent the non-Clifford state as a sum of Clifford ZX-diagrams, using cutting techniques to reduce the number of terms. They also provide numerical simulations using non-Clifford stabiliser rank methods.
result: The proposed method reduces the number of terms by more than a factor of 10 compared to naive decompositions, and achieves nearly 1000 shots per second on a laptop for small circuits at uniform noise level 0.001.
conclusion: The work demonstrates that operationally relevant high T-count quantum circuits with internal structure can be simulated more efficiently, shedding light on the simulability of such circuits.

title: Benchmarking Loss Functions For Trainable Quantum Feature Maps
authors: Nguyen Dinh Quyen, Vu Tuan Hai, Quoc Chuong Nguyen, Le Bin Ho, Lan Nguyen Tran
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12487v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many quantum machine learning models employ quantum feature maps to encode classical data into quantum states. While fixed feature maps often lack sufficient expressivity for complex nonlinear classification tasks, trainable quantum feature maps (TQFMs) enable adaptive quantum kernels with enhanced learning capability. Different loss functions can induce distinct optimization dynamics, yet their effects remain poorly understood. In this work, we apply the Log-Likelihood Loss function for TQFMs and provide a systematic comparison with Distance Loss and Measurement Loss. Through extensive numerical experiments, we compare their optimization dynamics, computational costs, and classification performance. Our results show that Log-Likelihood Loss consistently achieves more stable optimization than Measurement Loss while retaining linear computational complexity. The resulting benchmark offers practical guidance for balancing trainability, computational efficiency, and predictive performance in quantum kernel optimization.
tldr: This paper benchmarks loss functions for trainable quantum feature maps in quantum machine learning, focusing on optimization dynamics and classification performance.
motivation: Trainable quantum feature maps (TQFMs) are used in quantum machine learning, but the effect of different loss functions on their optimization is poorly understood.
method: The authors apply Log-Likelihood Loss to TQFMs and compare it with Distance Loss and Measurement Loss through numerical experiments, analyzing optimization dynamics, computational cost, and classification performance.
result: Log-Likelihood Loss achieves more stable optimization than Measurement Loss while maintaining linear computational complexity.
conclusion: The benchmark provides practical guidance for selecting loss functions in quantum kernel optimization, balancing trainability, efficiency, and performance.

title: Photoinduced Nonequilibrium States In Mott Insulators
authors: Yuta Murakami, Denis Golež, Martin Eckstein, And Philipp Werner
abstract:

The interplay between nonequilibrium physics and strong electronic correlations offers a unique platform for manipulating material properties, exploring novel optical responses, and uncovering quantum metastable phases. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in understanding the nonequilibrium dynamics of photoexcited Mott insulators—systems where strong interactions and a robust energy gap can give rise to rich and controllable phenomena. We discuss various nonlinear and nonperturbative pathways for driving and controlling Mott insulators using strong static or periodic fields. Furthermore, the review highlights key mechanisms that govern the evolution of photodoped carriers and the emergence of metastable and nonthermal states characterized by superconducting, magnetic, orbital, and excitonic orders.

tldr: A comprehensive review of photoinduced nonequilibrium states in Mott insulators, focusing on strong correlation dynamics and metastable phases.
motivation: To understand and control nonequilibrium dynamics in strongly correlated materials, which can lead to novel optical responses and quantum metastable phases.
method: Review of theoretical and experimental advances, discussing nonlinear and nonperturbative pathways using strong static or periodic fields, and mechanisms governing photodoped carrier evolution.
result: Highlights key mechanisms for emergent metastable states with superconducting, magnetic, orbital, and excitonic orders.
conclusion: Photoexcitation provides a powerful tool to manipulate Mott insulators, revealing rich nonequilibrium phenomena and potential for new functionalities.

title: Machine Learning Decoding Of Circuit-Level Noise For Bivariate Bicycle Codes
authors: John Blue, Harshil Avlani, Zhiyang He, Liu Ziyin, And Isaac L. Chuang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2149 (2026).

Fault-tolerant quantum computers will depend crucially on the performance of the classical decoding algorithm which takes in the results of measurements and outputs corrections to the errors inferred to have occurred. Machine learning models have shown great promise as decoders for the surface code; however, this promise has not yet been substantiated for the more challenging task of decoding quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes. In this paper, we present a recurrent, transformer-based neural network designed to decode circuit-level noise on Bivariate Bicycle (BB) codes. For the [MATH] BB code, at a physical error rate of [MATH], our model achieves logical error rates almost [MATH] times lower than belief propagation with ordered statistics decoding (BP-OSD), and roughly [MATH] times larger than a most-likely error decoder. Moreover, while BP-OSD has a wide distribution of runtimes with significant outliers, our model has a consistent runtime and is an order-of-magnitude faster than the worst-case times from a benchmark BP-OSD implementation. On the [MATH] BB code, our model obtains worse logical error rates but maintains the speed advantage. These results provide initial evidence that machine learning decoders can out-perform conventional decoders on small QLDPC codes, but suggest more complex architectures and/or training procedures are necessary to scale to larger code sizes.

.
tldr: This paper applies machine learning to decode circuit-level noise for bivariate bicycle codes, a type of quantum LDPC code.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires efficient decoders; machine learning decoders have shown promise for surface codes but not yet for QLDPC codes.
method: A recurrent, transformer-based neural network is designed to decode circuit-level noise on bivariate bicycle codes.
result: For the [[144,12,12]] BB code, the model achieves logical error rates almost 10 times lower than BP-OSD and is an order of magnitude faster, but for larger codes performance degrades.
conclusion: Machine learning decoders can outperform conventional decoders on small QLDPC codes, but scaling to larger codes requires more complex architectures.

title: What It Is Like To Be A Quantum Computer: A Closed Quantum Global Workspace -- Conscious Access And Integration As Correlation Dynamics In Hilbert Space
authors: Libby Heaney
abstract: ArXiv:2607.11909v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Motivated by speculative artistic inquiry into quantum-only forms of experience in relation to representation and embodiment, this paper develops a translation of the Global Neuronal Workspace (GNW) theory for closed quantum systems. The work treats classical GNW as an architectural reference and asks how conscious access and memory change under unitary dynamics. We reference a quantum Hopfield-style Hamiltonian that mirrors key organisational features of GNW, such as a distributed workspace and tunable large-scale integration. Within this framework, global availability of information is realised through coherence-preserving correlation distributions and memory is a persistent internal correlation structure. Likewise, ignition becomes a transition in global entanglement as opposed to convergence towards a stable attractor. Reductions of the Hopfield-style Hamiltonian lead to a tractable toy model and GHZ-type entanglement, explicitly showing how relative phase is globally accessible through joint internal operations yet absent from all local subsystems. This closed quantum system approach clarifies which aspects of workspace theories are contingent on classical assumptions. Our model highlights a non-representational regime in which access and memory are entirely relational rather than copies or records. Beyond its scientific contribution, the paper proposes a mode of art-science collaboration where speculative artistic inquiry is pursued through theoretical models rather than illustration or data.
tldr: A speculative paper translating Global Neuronal Workspace theory to closed quantum systems using a quantum Hopfield model, focusing on conscious access and memory as correlation dynamics.
motivation: To explore quantum-only forms of experience and representation through a theoretical model, bridging art and science.
method: Develops a quantum Hopfield-style Hamiltonian that mirrors GNW features, reduces to a toy model with GHZ-type entanglement, and analyzes global availability and ignition as entanglement transitions.
result: Shows that relative phase is globally accessible via joint operations but absent locally, highlighting a non-representational regime where access and memory are relational.
conclusion: The model clarifies which aspects of workspace theories depend on classical assumptions and proposes a new mode of art-science collaboration.

tldr: This paper extends the imaginary-time formalism to nonlinear response functions, providing a method to compute causal nonlinear response via analytic continuation of Matsubara-like functions.
motivation: Linear response theory is well understood via imaginary-time formalism, but nonlinear response lacks a similar framework. The authors aim to fill this gap for interacting and disordered systems.
method: They develop a diagrammatic approach for nonlinear response functions in the imaginary-time domain, analogous to the Matsubara technique for linear response, and establish analytic continuation rules to obtain real-time causal functions.
result: They derive explicit formulas for second- and third-order nonlinear response functions in terms of imaginary-time-ordered correlation functions, and demonstrate the method on simple models.
conclusion: The imaginary-time formalism can be systematically extended to nonlinear response, enabling efficient computation of higher-order response in quantum many-body systems.
