Nonlinear magnetic susceptibility measurements in the kagome spin ice HoAgGe reveal hidden time-reversal symmetry breaking in the ground states, reached via a three-dimensional XY universality class transition.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021043] Published Tue May 26, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the three-dimensional XY universality class and nonlinear magnetic susceptibility in a kagome ice compound HoAgGe, revealing hidden time-reversal symmetry breaking.
motivation: To understand the nature of the ground state and phase transition in the kagome spin ice HoAgGe, which exhibits a three-dimensional XY universality class transition.
method: Nonlinear magnetic susceptibility measurements and neutron scattering experiments were performed on single crystals of HoAgGe.
result: The measurements reveal hidden time-reversal symmetry breaking in the ground states, and the transition belongs to the three-dimensional XY universality class.
conclusion: The study provides insights into the magnetic properties of kagome ice compounds and the role of universality in phase transitions.

title: Robust Orbital-Selective Flat Bands In Layered Transition-Metal Oxyhalides At Room Temperature
authors: Xiangyu Luo, Ludovica Zullo, Sahaj Patel, Dongjin Oh, Willa Mihalyi-Koch, Emma Lian, Jiaruo Li, Qian Song, Asish K. Kundu, Anil Rajapitamahuni, Elio Vescovo, Natalia Olszowska, Rafał Kurleto, Dawid Wutke, Xavier Roy, Giorgio Sangiovanni, And Riccardo Comin
abstract:
Author(s): Xiangyu Luo, Ludovica Zullo, Sahaj Patel, Dongjin Oh, Willa Mihalyi-Koch, Emma Lian, Jiaruo Li, Qian Song, Asish K. Kundu, Anil Rajapitamahuni, Elio Vescovo, Natalia Olszowska, Rafał Kurleto, Dawid Wutke, Xavier Roy, Giorgio Sangiovanni, and Riccardo Comin

Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy of layered transition-metal oxyhalides reveals intrinsic flat bands that remain stable at room temperature, providing a tunable platform for investigating strongly correlated electron states.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021041] Published Thu May 21, 2026.
tldr: This paper reports the observation of robust orbital-selective flat bands in layered transition-metal oxyhalides at room temperature using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy.
motivation: Flat bands in strongly correlated materials can host exotic quantum phases, but most are only stable at low temperatures. The authors aim to find a room-temperature platform for studying such phenomena.
method: The authors synthesize layered transition-metal oxyhalides and characterize their electronic structure using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) and density functional theory (DFT) calculations.
result: They observe intrinsic flat bands that are orbital-selective and remain stable at room temperature, providing a tunable platform for strongly correlated electron states.
conclusion: This work demonstrates a new material platform for investigating flat-band physics at room temperature, which could enable studies of correlated phenomena without cryogenic constraints.

title: Probing Quantum Anomalous Hall States In Twisted Bilayer ${\mathrm{WSe}}_{2}$ Via Attractive Polaron Spectroscopy
authors: Beini Gao, Mahdi Ghafariasl, Mahmoud Jalali Mehrabad, Tsung-Sheng Huang, Lifu Zhang, Deric Session, Pranshoo Upadhyay, Rundong Ma, Ghadah Alshalan, Daniel Suarez, Supratik Sarkar, Suji Park, Houk Jang, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Ming Xie, You Zhou, And Mohammad Hafezi

Magneto-optical spectroscopy of twisted WSe

tldr: This paper reports magneto-optical spectroscopy of twisted bilayer WSe2, revealing a quantum anomalous Hall phase and electric-field control of magnetic order.
motivation: To probe and control quantum anomalous Hall states in twisted bilayer WSe2, a moiré material with potential for topological phases.
method: Attractive polaron spectroscopy combined with magneto-optical measurements under varying electric fields.
result: Observation of a spontaneous quantum anomalous Hall phase and electric-field-driven transitions between ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic orders.
conclusion: Twisted bilayer WSe2 is a platform for studying and controlling quantum anomalous Hall states, with implications for topological electronics.

Multimodal optical characterization of Ni
[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021030] Published Fri May 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper reports the observation of intertwined polar, chiral, and ferro-rotational orders in a homo-ferro-rotational insulator using multimodal optical characterization.
motivation: To understand the coupling between different ferroic orders (polar, chiral, ferro-rotational) in a single material and the resulting complex domain structures.
method: Multimodal optical characterization techniques were applied to Ni₂MnBO₅ to identify and distinguish the different ferroic orders and their domain walls.
result: A uniform ferro-rotational state was identified that couples polarity and chirality, leading to the formation of complex mixed-type domain walls.
conclusion: The study reveals a new type of multiferroic order with intertwined ferroic properties, which may have implications for multifunctional materials.

title: Stealthy-Hyperuniform Wave Dynamics In Two-Dimensional Photonic Crystals
authors: Maria Barsukova, Zeyu Zhang, Brian Gould, Koorosh Sadri, Christian Rosiek, Søren Stobbe, Jonas Karcher, And Mikael C. Rechtsman
abstract:
Author(s): Maria Barsukova, Zeyu Zhang, Brian Gould, Koorosh Sadri, Christian Rosiek, Søren Stobbe, Jonas Karcher, and Mikael C. Rechtsman

While disordered stealthy hyperuniform materials are expected to be largely transparent within a particular range of wavelengths, new experiments on large-scale silicon photonic crystals reveal unexpected residual scattering driven by radiative loss.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021028] Published Thu May 07, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies wave dynamics in two-dimensional photonic crystals with stealthy hyperuniform disorder, revealing unexpected residual scattering due to radiative loss.
motivation: Stealthy hyperuniform materials are expected to be transparent in certain wavelength ranges, but experiments show unexpected scattering that needs explanation.
method: Large-scale silicon photonic crystals are fabricated and characterized experimentally, with theoretical modeling of radiative loss effects.
result: Residual scattering is observed and attributed to radiative loss, contradicting the expectation of transparency.
conclusion: The findings highlight the role of radiative loss in disordered photonic crystals, important for photonic device design.

title: Ballistic Spin Valve In Graphene Realized Via Electron Optics
authors: Daniel Burrow, Oktay Deveci, Rares Dragomir, Thomas Thomson, And Ivan J. Vera-Marun
abstract:
Author(s): Daniel Burrow, Oktay Deveci, Rares Dragomir, Thomas Thomson, and Ivan J. Vera-Marun

Transverse magnetic focusing in encapsulated graphene reveals gate-tunable ballistic spin transport, providing a mechanism for coherent spin control through spin-dependent electron optics.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021029] Published Thu May 07, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a ballistic spin valve in graphene using transverse magnetic focusing and electron optics.
motivation: To achieve coherent spin control and spin-dependent electron optics in graphene for spintronic applications.
method: Transverse magnetic focusing in encapsulated graphene reveals gate-tunable ballistic spin transport.
result: Observation of ballistic spin transport and coherent spin control via spin-dependent electron optics.
conclusion: The work provides a mechanism for spin control in graphene, relevant to spintronics but not to the specified research directions.

title: Grand Challenge Of Quantum Applications
authors: Ryan Babbush, Robbie King, Sergio Boixo, William Huggins, Tanuj Khattar, Guang Hao Low, Jarrod R. Mcclean, Thomas O’brien, And Nicholas C. Rubin
abstract:
Author(s): Ryan Babbush, Robbie King, Sergio Boixo, William Huggins, Tanuj Khattar, Guang Hao Low, Jarrod R. McClean, Thomas O’Brien, and Nicholas C. Rubin

A proposed five-stage framework outlines the path to useful quantum computing, detailing the scientific milestones required to bridge the gap between theory and real-world utility.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020101] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a five-stage framework for achieving useful quantum computing, focusing on scientific milestones rather than specific technical results.
motivation: To bridge the gap between theoretical quantum computing and real-world utility by outlining a structured path forward.
method: The authors present a conceptual framework with five stages, each defined by key scientific and engineering milestones.
result: A high-level roadmap for quantum computing development is provided, but no novel technical contributions or experimental results are reported.
conclusion: The framework serves as a guide for the field but does not advance any specific direction in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: 2d Van Der Waals Magnets: From Fundamental Physics To Applications
authors: Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, And Nuh Gedik
abstract:
Author(s): Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, and Nuh Gedik

Scientific discovery is often described as walking into a dark room and turning on the light. The discovery of 2D magnetism in van der Waals materials in 2016 was one such leap forward, removing one spatial dimension from macroscopic materials. The study of 2D magnets has challenged established theories and uncovered new phenomena. This review summarizes the current state of knowledge of magnetic phenomena in 2D van der Waals materials. The field encompasses not just the traditional study of ferromagnets and antiferromagnets but also topology, quantum and nonequilibrium dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons and spintronics, and the interaction of magnetism with light, phonons, and electric fields (multiferroics). The field is actively evolving, expanding theoretical understanding, materials capabilities, and experimental phenomenology while opening new directions for application.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025003] Published Wed May 27, 2026.
tldr: A review of 2D van der Waals magnets covering fundamental physics and applications.
motivation: To summarize the current state of knowledge and recent discoveries in 2D magnetism.
method: Review of experimental and theoretical studies on 2D van der Waals magnetic materials.
result: The field encompasses ferromagnets, antiferromagnets, topology, quantum dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons, spintronics, and interactions with light, phonons, and electric fields.
conclusion: The field is actively evolving and opening new directions for applications.

title: Radiation Forces And Torques In Optics And Acoustics
authors: Ivan Toftul, Sebastian Golat, Francisco J. Rodríguez-Fortuño, Franco Nori, Yuri Kivshar, And Konstantin Y. Bliokh
abstract:
Author(s): Ivan Toftul, Sebastian Golat, Francisco J. Rodríguez-Fortuño, Franco Nori, Yuri Kivshar, and Konstantin Y. Bliokh

This review presents a unified perspective of how local energy, momentum, and spin densities in optical and acoustic wave fields induce forces and torques on particles—a topic that has captivated researchers for centuries. Applications discussed include trapping and manipulation of atoms and nanoparticles by light, sorting of biological cells by the combination of acoustics and microfluidics, and pulling forces that draw particles against the direction of wave propagation.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025002] Published Thu Apr 30, 2026.
tldr: This review unifies the description of radiation forces and torques in optical and acoustic fields, focusing on momentum and spin densities.
motivation: Understanding how wave fields exert forces and torques on particles is fundamental for applications like optical trapping and acoustic manipulation.
method: The authors present a unified theoretical framework based on local energy, momentum, and spin densities in optical and acoustic waves.
result: They show that both optical and acoustic forces and torques can be described by similar conservation laws and stress tensors.
conclusion: The unified perspective aids in designing advanced particle manipulation techniques across optics and acoustics.

title: Exactly Solvable Quantum Many-body Dynamics From Space-time Duality
authors: Bruno Bertini, Pieter W. Claeys, And Tomaž Prosen
abstract:
Author(s): Bruno Bertini, Pieter W. Claeys, and Tomaž Prosen

Computing quantum dynamics in many-body systems is notoriously difficult. In the past decade, there has been a fundamental advance based on discretizing the time evolution of lattice systems, by analogy with digital computation. Since space is already discrete on a lattice, treating space and time on the same footing avoids the mathematical complications of continuous space-time quantum field theories. This review focuses on how this space-time duality plays out in the dynamics of interacting many-body systems and the intrinsic relationship with special kinds of lattices termed brickwork quantum circuits. From this pedagogical review, readers will learn how this far-reaching analogy with quantum computation lies at the heart of a unified view of dynamical evolution of quantum many-body systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025001] Published Wed Apr 15, 2026.
tldr: A pedagogical review of exactly solvable quantum many-body dynamics using space-time duality and brickwork quantum circuits.
motivation: Computing quantum dynamics in many-body systems is notoriously difficult; this review aims to provide a unified view of dynamical evolution by treating space and time on the same footing.
method: The review focuses on space-time duality in interacting many-body systems and its relationship with brickwork quantum circuits, drawing analogies with digital computation.
result: The paper presents a pedagogical exposition of how space-time duality enables exact solvability of certain quantum many-body dynamics.
conclusion: Space-time duality offers a powerful framework for understanding quantum many-body dynamics, with deep connections to quantum computation.

title: Kagome Metals
authors: Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, And Stephen D. Wilson
abstract:
Author(s): Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, and Stephen D. Wilson

The kagome lattice is a two-dimensional tiling of hexagons and triangles named after a Japanese basket weaving technique. Its geometry gives rise to highly frustrated interactions and interference effects experienced by electrons and their multiple degrees of freedom. In metals, the exploration of materials with kagome conduction networks is driven by predictions of realizing new electronic states where these interference effects are dominant, amplifying electronic interactions and many-body effects. In these kagome metals, these amplified correlation effects in combination with spin-orbit coupling and other forms of frustration have given rise to a wealth of phenomena beyond expectations. These include unusual states and responses born from topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, sublattice interference effects at saddle points such as unconventional superconductivity, orbital antiferromagnetism and flux phases, amplified anomalous Hall effects, and electronic nematic states. This review examines the theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, with the aim of elucidating fundamental mechanisms underlying the observed exotic phenomena.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015002] Published Thu Feb 12, 2026.
tldr: A review of kagome metals, focusing on exotic electronic states arising from the kagome lattice geometry.
motivation: To understand the fundamental mechanisms behind unusual phenomena in kagome metals, such as unconventional superconductivity and topological flat bands.
method: Review of theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, analyzing electronic structure and many-body effects.
result: Identifies key phenomena including topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, and sublattice interference effects.
conclusion: Kagome metals provide a platform for realizing novel electronic states driven by frustration and interference.

title: Field Theories And Quantum Methods For Stochastic Reaction-diffusion Systems
authors: Mauricio J. Del Razo, Tommaso Lamma, And Wout Merbis
abstract:
Author(s): Mauricio J. del Razo, Tommaso Lamma, and Wout Merbis

The exchange of energy and molecules in a living cell, the spread of opinions through a society, and the flow of traffic in a crowded city are very different phenomena, yet they are all examples of complex systems composed of many agents that interact with each other and exchange energy or particles with the environment. These systems can be modeled as stochastic reaction-diffusion systems. In this pedagogical review, the authors apply powerful field-theoretic methods to these systems, unifying diverse approaches under a single framework. The methods are useful for handling chemical systems but also have applications in a wide range of areas such as ecology and epidemiology.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015001] Published Thu Jan 22, 2026.
tldr: A pedagogical review applying field-theoretic methods to stochastic reaction-diffusion systems in complex systems like ecology and epidemiology.
motivation: To unify diverse approaches for modeling stochastic reaction-diffusion systems across different fields.
method: Uses field-theoretic methods (e.g., Doi-Peliti formalism) to derive and solve master equations for reaction-diffusion processes.
result: Provides a unified framework for analyzing stochastic dynamics in chemical, ecological, and epidemiological systems.
conclusion: Field-theoretic methods are powerful tools for studying stochastic reaction-diffusion systems, with broad applicability beyond physics.

title: Spin-glass Dynamics: Experiment, Theory, And Simulation
authors: E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, And D. Yllanes
abstract:
Author(s): E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, and D. Yllanes

This review updates the field of spin glasses with broad application to a large variety of physical systems. In particular, this review tracks the progress of experiment, theory, and large-scale simulations. It highlights the importance of their synergy, from the inception of the field to the present day, and includes future opportunities for research.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045005] Published Mon Dec 15, 2025.
tldr: A review of spin-glass dynamics covering experiment, theory, and simulation.
motivation: To provide an updated overview of spin-glass research and highlight the synergy between experimental, theoretical, and computational approaches.
method: Review of experimental techniques, theoretical models, and large-scale simulations of spin glasses.
result: Summarizes key advances in understanding spin-glass dynamics and identifies future research opportunities.
conclusion: Spin-glass dynamics remain a rich field with broad applications, and continued interdisciplinary collaboration is essential.

title: Kitaev Quantum Spin Liquids
authors: Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, And Hae-Young Kee
abstract:
Author(s): Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, and Hae-Young Kee

Frustration in spin systems can prevent ordering even at =0, creating quantum spin liquids that have been sought since Anderson’s pioneering work in 1973 and his influential 1987 paper connecting them to high-temperature superconductivity. Kitaev’s solvable spin-1/2 models on a honeycomb lattice brought renewed attention to this field, with Jackeli and Khaliullin later revealing how to engineer Kitaev interactions in real materials. This review highlights theoretical and experimental developments in Kitaev spin liquids, emphasizing leading candidate materials and their broad topological properties such as chiral edge modes. Consequently, it provides essential insights for both experimentalists and theorists working on quantum spin liquid problems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045003] Published Wed Dec 03, 2025.
tldr: A review of Kitaev quantum spin liquids, focusing on candidate materials and topological properties.
motivation: To provide an overview of theoretical and experimental progress in Kitaev spin liquids, which are a type of quantum spin liquid with potential applications in topological quantum computing.
method: The paper reviews theoretical models (Kitaev honeycomb model) and experimental realizations in materials, highlighting chiral edge modes and other topological features.
result: The review summarizes key candidate materials and their properties, emphasizing the broad topological phenomena observed.
conclusion: Kitaev spin liquids are a rich field with many open questions, and the review serves as a guide for future research.

title: The Ups And Downs Of Internal Conversion
authors: Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, And Salvy P. Russo
abstract:
Author(s): Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, and Salvy P. Russo

This review examines the theoretical methods used to describe the photophysical process of internal conversion in quantum systems. These models explore all facets of the nonradiative mechanism, and the review presents an outlook on how they can be incorporated in studies relevant to applications, for example, in photonics and energy harvesting.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035003] Published Tue Sep 16, 2025.
tldr: A review of theoretical methods for internal conversion in quantum systems, focusing on nonradiative transitions and their applications in photonics and energy harvesting.
motivation: Internal conversion is a fundamental photophysical process, and understanding its theoretical underpinnings is important for applications in photonics and energy harvesting.
method: The paper reviews various theoretical models describing internal conversion, including nonradiative mechanisms and their incorporation into application-oriented studies.
result: The review provides an overview of current theoretical approaches and an outlook on future directions for integrating these models into practical applications.
conclusion: Theoretical methods for internal conversion are advancing, but further development is needed to fully exploit them in photonics and energy harvesting technologies.

title: Colloquium: Quantum Properties And Functionalities Of Magnetic Skyrmions
authors: Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, And Christos Panagopoulos
abstract:
Author(s): Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, and Christos Panagopoulos

Skyrmions are topological field configurations that were first discussed in the context of high-energy theory. In recent years, skyrmionic spin patterns in solid-state systems have received much attention, in part for their promising application potential. This Colloquium discusses quantum-mechanical aspects of such magnetic skyrmions, both for the interactions that underlie skyrmion formation and for quantum features of the skyrmions themselves.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 031001] Published Tue Jul 08, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews quantum properties and functionalities of magnetic skyrmions, focusing on their topological nature and potential applications.
motivation: Magnetic skyrmions are promising for spintronic devices, but their quantum aspects are less explored; this review aims to bridge that gap.
method: The paper surveys theoretical and experimental work on skyrmion formation, quantum tunneling, and quantum-classical correspondence.
result: It highlights quantum effects such as skyrmion tunneling and quantum fluctuations, and discusses how these could enable new functionalities.
conclusion: Quantum skyrmionics is an emerging field with potential for novel quantum technologies, but many open questions remain.

title: Spin-dependent Exotic Interactions
authors: Lei Cong, Wei Ji, Pavel Fadeev, Filip Ficek, Min Jiang, Victor V. Flambaum, Haosen Guan, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Mikhail G. Kozlov, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, And Dmitry Budker
abstract:
Author(s): Lei Cong, Wei Ji, Pavel Fadeev, Filip Ficek, Min Jiang, Victor V. Flambaum, Haosen Guan, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Mikhail G. Kozlov, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, and Dmitry Budker

This review presents a comprehensive summary of theoretical investigations and experimental searches for spin-dependent interactions beyond the standard model. These interactions may be mediated by various types of exotic bosons, and their existence and properties may, in turn, explain the nature of dark matter and dark energy. The described experiments also probe the discrete fundamental symmetries of nature.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025005] Published Tue Jun 24, 2025.
tldr: A comprehensive review of theoretical and experimental searches for spin-dependent exotic interactions beyond the standard model, including their possible mediation by exotic bosons and implications for dark matter and dark energy.
motivation: To understand the nature of dark matter and dark energy, and to probe discrete fundamental symmetries, it is crucial to investigate spin-dependent interactions beyond the standard model.
method: The paper reviews theoretical frameworks for spin-dependent exotic interactions and summarizes experimental searches using various techniques such as atomic magnetometry, torsion balances, and astrophysical observations.
result: The review provides a comprehensive summary of current constraints on spin-dependent interactions and discusses future experimental prospects.
conclusion: Spin-dependent exotic interactions remain a promising avenue for discovering new physics, and further experimental and theoretical work is needed to explore their implications for dark matter and fundamental symmetries.

title: Colloquium: Materials That Exceed Classical Thermodynamic Bounds On Properties
authors: Roderic S. Lakes
abstract:
Author(s): Roderic S. Lakes

Classical thermodynamic bounds provide constraints on values that are expected in measurements of certain physical properties. In a variety of fields, some measurements exceed these bounds. This apparent violation of thermodynamics arises because the measurements are made in ways that violate the underlying assumptions made when deriving these bounds. This Colloquium describes a wide variety of circumstances where such violations occur and which of the underlying assumptions are violated in each case. It also describes how interesting material properties can be developed using materials designed to violate these assumptions.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021002] Published Wed May 14, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews materials that appear to exceed classical thermodynamic bounds on properties, explaining the violations by examining underlying assumptions.
motivation: Classical thermodynamic bounds are often assumed to be fundamental, but some measurements exceed them; understanding why can lead to novel materials.
method: The paper surveys a wide variety of materials and phenomena where bounds are exceeded, analyzing which assumptions (e.g., equilibrium, linear response) are violated.
result: It identifies that violations occur because measurements are made under conditions that invalidate the assumptions of the bounds, and shows how to design materials that exploit these violations.
conclusion: Apparent violations of thermodynamic bounds are not actual violations but arise from misapplication of the bounds; this insight can guide development of materials with extreme properties.

title: Colloquium: Synthetic Quantum Matter In Nonstandard Geometries
authors: Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, And Christof Weitenberg
abstract:
Author(s): Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, and Christof Weitenberg

This Colloquium presents ways to implement fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions in atomic, photonic, and electronic systems. The study of quantum many-body physics in these exotic geometries permits simulation of phenomena from topology in condensed matter to models of gravity and cosmology.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 011001] Published Tue Mar 25, 2025.
tldr: A colloquium review on implementing fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions in atomic, photonic, and electronic systems for quantum many-body physics.
motivation: To explore exotic geometries that enable simulation of phenomena from condensed matter topology to gravity and cosmology.
method: Review of experimental and theoretical approaches for realizing nonstandard geometries in various quantum platforms.
result: Summarizes current capabilities and challenges in engineering synthetic quantum matter in fractal, curved, and higher-dimensional spaces.
conclusion: These nonstandard geometries offer new avenues for quantum simulation but are not directly aligned with the user's core research directions.

title: Massive Quantum Systems As Interfaces Of Quantum Mechanics And Gravity
authors: Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, And Clara C. Wanjura
abstract:
Author(s): Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, and Clara C. Wanjura

The authors review theories and experimental state-of-the-art efforts to study the effects of gravity on massive quantum systems. Classical gravity is the least precisely tested natural force and may be addressed via precision quantum probes. Experiments testing whether the quantum nature of gravity causes decoherence and collapse of matter-wave functions and whether it can mediate entanglement between separate massive particles are underway, and their results will guide the theoretical description of gravity effects on a laboratory scale.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015003] Published Thu Feb 13, 2025.
tldr: A review of theoretical and experimental efforts to study gravity's effects on massive quantum systems, including tests of quantum gravity and gravity-induced entanglement.
motivation: Classical gravity is the least precisely tested natural force, and massive quantum systems may serve as probes to study gravity's quantum nature.
method: The paper reviews theoretical frameworks (e.g., decoherence models, entanglement mediation) and experimental approaches (matter-wave interferometry, optomechanics) for testing gravity with quantum systems.
result: Current experiments are underway to detect gravity-induced decoherence and entanglement, which will guide the theoretical description of gravity at the laboratory scale.
conclusion: Massive quantum systems offer a promising avenue to explore the interface of quantum mechanics and gravity, but the field is still in early stages.

title: On The Significance Of Wigner’s Friend In Contexts Beyond Quantum Foundations
authors: Caroline L. Jones And Markus P. Mueller
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2147 (2026).

There has been a surge of recent interest in the Wigner's Friend paradox, sparking several novel thought experiments and no-go theorems. The main narrative has been that Wigner's Friend highlights a counterintuitive feature that is unique to quantum theory, and which is closely related to the quantum measurement problem. Here, we challenge this view. We argue that the gist of the Wigner's Friend paradox can be reproduced without assuming quantum physics, and that it underlies a much broader class of enigmas in the foundations of physics and philosophy. To show this, we first consider several recently proposed Extended Wigner's Friend scenarios, and demonstrate that some of their implications for the absoluteness of observations can be reproduced by classical thought experiments that involve the duplication of agents. Crucially, some of these classical scenarios are technologically much easier to implement than their quantum counterparts. Then, we argue that the essential structural ingredient of all these scenarios is a feature that we call "Restriction A": that a physical theory cannot give us a probabilistic description of the observations of all agents. Finally, we argue that this difficulty is at the core of other puzzles in the foundations of physics and philosophy, and demonstrate this explicitly for cosmology's Boltzmann brain problem. Our analysis suggests that Wigner's Friend should be studied in a larger context, addressing a frontier of human knowledge beyond quantum foundations: to obtain reliable predictions for experiments in which these predictions can be privately but not intersubjectively verified.

.
tldr: The paper argues that the Wigner's Friend paradox is not unique to quantum theory but can be reproduced classically, and relates it to broader foundational puzzles.
motivation: To challenge the view that Wigner's Friend highlights a uniquely quantum feature and to show its relevance to other foundational problems.
method: The authors construct classical thought experiments that mimic extended Wigner's Friend scenarios and identify a common structural feature called 'Restriction A'.
result: They demonstrate that some implications of Wigner's Friend can be reproduced classically, and that the paradox shares structure with the Boltzmann brain problem.
conclusion: Wigner's Friend should be studied in a broader context beyond quantum foundations, addressing issues of private versus intersubjective verification.

title: Qubit Operations Using A Modular Optical System Engineered With PyOpticL: A code-to-CAD Optical Layout Tool
authors: Jacob Myers, Christopher Caron, Nishat Helaly, Zhenyu Wei, Justin Oh, Zack Gotobed, Kotaro Yabe, And Robert J. Niffenegger
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2135 (2026).

Complex optical design is hindered by conventional piecewise setup, which prevents modularization and therefore abstraction of subsystems at the circuit level. This limits multiple fields that require complex optics systems, including quantum computing with atoms and trapped ions, because their optical systems are not scalable. We present an open-source Python library for optical layout (PyOpticL) which uses beam-path simulation and dynamic beam-path routing for quick and easy optical layout by placing optical elements along the beam path without a priori specification, enabling adaptive, path-based layouts with automatic routing and connectivity. We use PyOpticL to create modular `drop-in' optical baseplates for common optical subsystems used in atomic and molecular optics (AMO) experiments including laser sources, frequency and intensity modulation, and locking to an atomic reference for stabilization. We demonstrate this minimal working example of a dynamic full laser system for strontium trapped ions by using it for laser cooling, qubit state detection, and over 99% fidelity single-qubit gates with 3D printed baseplates. This enables a new paradigm of design abstraction layers for engineering optical systems leveraging modular baseplates, as they can be used for any wavelength in the system and enables scaling up the underlying optical systems for quantum computers. This new open-source hardware and software code-to-CAD library seeks to foster open-source collaborative hardware and systems design across numerous fields of research including AMO physics and quantum computing with neutral atoms and trapped ions.

.
tldr: This paper presents PyOpticL, an open-source Python library for modular optical layout, and demonstrates its use for building a laser system for trapped-ion qubit operations.
motivation: Complex optical design in quantum computing with atoms and trapped ions is hindered by conventional piecewise setup, which prevents modularization and scalability.
method: The authors developed PyOpticL, a Python library that uses beam-path simulation and dynamic routing to enable adaptive, path-based layouts. They created modular optical baseplates for common subsystems and demonstrated a full laser system for strontium trapped ions.
result: The system achieved over 99% fidelity single-qubit gates and was used for laser cooling and qubit state detection, showing the feasibility of modular optical design.
conclusion: PyOpticL enables a new paradigm of design abstraction for optical systems, fostering open-source collaborative hardware design for AMO physics and quantum computing.

title: Strain-driven Transition From Correlated Insulating To Semimetallic States In Twisted-bilayer Graphene
authors: Lishuai Guo, Abulimiti Yasen, Mei Xiang, Wenliang Zhu And Minghu Pan
abstract: We investigate the interplay between Coulomb interaction and uniaxial heterostrain in twisted bilayer graphene (TBG) using a self-consistent Hartree–Fock (HF) approach projected onto the flat bands. For integer filling factors in the range of , we find that heterostrain strongly reconstructs the low-energy band structure and suppresses interaction-induced insulating gaps. As strain magnitude increases, the flat-band bandwidth is substantially enhanced, leading to an increased kinetic energy. The bandwidth enhancement effectively weakens the interaction strength relative to kinetic energy, resulting in the suppression of HF gaps and the emergence of semimetallic (SM) states. The strain effect can be primarily controlled by the filling factor, as well as the strain direction. At moderate strain strengths around 0.3% for , it can drive transitions between correlated insulating and SM states. In contrast, for , the HF gaps becomes negligible and the system remains essentially SM; both the strain direction and magnitude have negligible influence. Our results demonstrate that uniaxial heterostrain serves as an effective and versatile parameter for tuning correlated phases in TBG through the interplay of lattice deformation and Coulomb interactions.
tldr: This paper studies strain-driven transitions between correlated insulating and semimetallic states in twisted bilayer graphene using Hartree-Fock calculations.
motivation: Understanding how uniaxial heterostrain affects correlated phases in twisted bilayer graphene, which is a key material in condensed matter physics.
method: Self-consistent Hartree-Fock approach projected onto flat bands to compute band structure and interaction gaps under varying strain.
result: Strain enhances bandwidth and suppresses insulating gaps, driving transitions to semimetallic states; effect depends on filling factor and strain direction.
conclusion: Uniaxial heterostrain is an effective tuning parameter for correlated phases in twisted bilayer graphene.

title: Sorting Prolate And Oblate Spheroids With A Diatomic Gas In A Magnetic Field
authors: Ruben Lier
abstract: For a gas of diatomic particles with a nonzero magnetic moment, the Senftleben–Beenakker effect implies that transport can be affected by a magnetic field even when the particles are charge neutral. In such a gas, two independent anisotropic odd viscosities are allowed by symmetry and can have opposite signs. We study the resulting odd-viscous Stokes flow around spheroids in the regime where the odd viscosities are small compared to the shear viscosity. Using a perturbative expansion around the spherical solution and the Lorentz reciprocal theorem, we compute the lift forces on oblate and prolate spheroids for general values of the two odd viscosity coefficients. We show that the resulting Hall angles can differ for oblate and prolate spheroids, implying that sedimentation in a diatomic gas subject to a background magnetic field can separate particles according to shape.
tldr: This paper studies odd-viscous Stokes flow around spheroids in a diatomic gas under a magnetic field, showing shape-based separation via Hall angles.
motivation: Understanding how odd viscosities affect particle transport in neutral gases with magnetic moments, enabling shape-based separation.
method: Perturbative expansion around spherical solution and Lorentz reciprocal theorem to compute lift forces on spheroids for general odd viscosity coefficients.
result: Hall angles differ for oblate and prolate spheroids, allowing shape separation during sedimentation in a magnetic field.
conclusion: Odd viscosities in diatomic gases can be exploited to separate particles by shape, with potential applications in particle sorting.

title: Physical Sampling For Computational Photography
authors: Ni Chen And David J Brady
abstract: The standard model of photography is that lenses form images and focal planes capture those images. Over the past two decades, however, cameras have been transformed from devices that record focal images into analog-to-digital converters that transform massively parallel optical signals into serial electronic data. Under this new model, one may choose to maximize the quality and quantity of captured information, rather than focal image quality. Here we review the nature of the optical data stream and consider lens and focal plane designs that improve information capture capacity. After maximizing information capacity, the challenge of converting this information to digital data requires novel read-out and compression. We review strategies for approaching physical information limits under realistic size, power, and bandwidth constraints. Multiscale monocentric (spherical primary optics combined with arrays of secondary micro-cameras, each imaging a narrow subfield) and array lens architectures relax unfavorable geometric scaling by trading monolithic optics for co-designed system-level integration (jointly optimized optics, focal-plane, and readout subsystems). Metaoptic and mode-sorting focal plane filters implement richer projection operators that sample spectral, polarimetric, and coherence features without requiring exhaustive scanning. Finally, because readout and computation dominate energy at high throughput, we highlight architectures that perform dimensionality reduction before (or during) digitization, including integrated photonic encoders and multilayer optical projections coupled to detection and learned decoding. Together, these developments motivate a shift from cameras optimized to produce 2D images toward cameras engineered as end-to-end information channels, co-designing optics, focal-plane, and readout to deliver more task-relevant measurements per photon and per joule.
tldr: This paper reviews computational photography architectures that optimize information capture and compression under physical constraints, but does not address quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To improve camera design by maximizing information capacity and energy efficiency, moving beyond traditional focal imaging.
method: Reviews multiscale optics, metaoptic filters, and integrated photonic encoders that perform dimensionality reduction before digitization.
result: Proposes co-designed optics, focal-plane, and readout subsystems to deliver more task-relevant measurements per photon and per joule.
conclusion: Cameras should be engineered as end-to-end information channels rather than simple image recorders.

title: Green’s Function Methods For Computing Supercurrents In Josephson Junctions
authors: Eduardo R Mucciolo, Jouko Nieminen, Xiao Xiao, Wei-Chi Chiu, Michael N Leuenberger And Arun Bansil
abstract: Interest in Josephson junctions (JJs) has increased rapidly in recent years not only because of their use in qubits and other quantum devices but also due to the unique physics supported by the JJs. The advent of various novel quantum materials for both the barrier region and the superconducting leads has led to the possibility of adding new functionalities to the JJs. Thus, there is a growing need for accurate modeling of the JJs and related systems to enable their predictive control and atomistic level understanding. This review presents an in-depth discussion of a Green’s-function-based formalism for computing supercurrents in JJs. The formulation is tailored for large-scale atomistic simulations and encompasses both dc and ac supercurrents. We hope that this review will provide a timely and comprehensive reference for researchers as well as beginning practitioners interested in Green’s-function-based methods to model supercurrents in JJs.
tldr: A review of Green's function methods for computing supercurrents in Josephson junctions, focusing on large-scale atomistic simulations.
motivation: Josephson junctions are key components in qubits and quantum devices, and accurate modeling is needed for predictive control and atomistic understanding.
method: The paper presents a Green's-function-based formalism tailored for large-scale atomistic simulations to compute both dc and ac supercurrents.
result: The formalism enables accurate modeling of supercurrents in Josephson junctions with novel quantum materials.
conclusion: The review serves as a comprehensive reference for researchers and practitioners interested in Green's-function-based modeling of supercurrents.

title: Unlocking Complex Optical Vortices With Flat Optics
authors: Hammad Ahmed, Shumei Chen, Xibin Yang And Xianzhong Chen
abstract: Optical vortices (OVs) possess spiral wavefronts and quantized orbital angular momentum (OAM), allowing them to act as key carriers of information and enabling light to possess high-dimensional degrees of freedom. In the past decade, there has been a growing interest in investigating complex OVs. Nevertheless, conventional methods for generating such beams are limited by bulky setups, high costs, and restricted control. Optical metasurfaces have emerged as promising candidates to overcome these challenges in a compact and cost-effective platform with enhanced control. This review begins by presenting an advanced platform designed for manipulating OVs and then discusses emerging types of OVs, including composite, grafted, and comb-like structured light beams, as well as multispectral and arbitrarily shaped OVs, along with nonlinear metasurface approaches. Next, we review the recent progress in OAM detection and mode discrimination, highlighting current challenges for high-capacity OAM systems. After that, we emphasize key applications ranging from OAM-based holography for optical encryption to super-resolution microscopy, structured-light trapping, and quantum state engineering. Finally, we critically identify the key challenges and future prospects for metasurface-enabled OV technologies.
tldr: A review of metasurface-based generation and detection of complex optical vortices for high-dimensional information encoding.
motivation: Conventional methods for generating complex optical vortices are bulky and costly; metasurfaces offer a compact, cost-effective platform with enhanced control.
method: The paper reviews recent progress in metasurface designs for generating composite, grafted, comb-like, multispectral, and arbitrarily shaped optical vortices, as well as OAM detection and mode discrimination techniques.
result: Metasurface-enabled OV technologies enable applications in OAM-based holography, super-resolution microscopy, structured-light trapping, and quantum state engineering.
conclusion: Metasurfaces provide a promising platform for complex OV manipulation, but challenges remain in scalability, efficiency, and integration for high-capacity OAM systems.

title: Chiral Graviton Modes In Fermionic Fractional Chern Insulators
authors: Min Long, Zeno Bacciconi, Hongyu Lu, Hernan B Xavier, Zi Yang Meng And Marcello Dalmonte
abstract: Chiral graviton modes are hallmark collective excitations of fractional quantum Hall (FQH) liquids. However, their existence on the lattice, where continuum symmetries that protect them from decay are lost, is still an open and urgent question, especially considering the recent advances in the realization of fractional Chern insulators (FCI) in transition metal dichalcogenides and rhombohedral pentalayer graphene. Here we present a comprehensive theoretical and numerical study of graviton-modes in fermionic FCI, and thoroughly demonstrate their existence. We first derive a lattice stress tensor operator in the context of the fermionic Harper–Hofstadter (HH) model which captures the graviton in the flat band limit. Importantly, we discover that such lattice stress-tensor operators are deeply connected to correlation hole dynamics, readily generalizable to generic Chern bands. We then explicitly show the adiabatic connection between FQH and FCI chiral graviton modes by interpolating from a low flux HH model to a Checkerboard lattice model that hosts a topological flat band. In particular, using state-of-the-art matrix product state and exact diagonalization simulations, we provide strong evidence that chiral graviton modes are long-lived excitations in FCIs despite the lack of continuous symmetries and the scattering with a two-magnetoroton continuum. By means of a careful finite-size analysis, we show that the lattice generates an intrinsic decay rate for the graviton mode which is small compared to its energy. We discuss the relevance of our results for the exploration of graviton modes in FCI phases realized in solid state settings, experimental utility on diagnosis of fractional topological phases, as well as cold atom experiments.
tldr: This paper studies chiral graviton modes in fractional Chern insulators, a topic in condensed matter physics with no direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To determine whether chiral graviton modes, hallmark excitations of fractional quantum Hall liquids, exist in lattice fractional Chern insulators despite the lack of continuous symmetries.
method: Derives a lattice stress tensor operator for the Harper-Hofstadter model, uses matrix product state and exact diagonalization simulations to study the adiabatic connection between FQH and FCI graviton modes.
result: Provides strong evidence that chiral graviton modes are long-lived excitations in FCIs, with a small intrinsic decay rate compared to their energy.
conclusion: The results are relevant for exploring graviton modes in FCI phases in solid-state and cold atom experiments, but do not advance quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Vortex Solitons In Disclination Quasicrystals
authors: Hua Zhong, Yaroslav V Kartashov, Yongdong Li, Fangwei Ye And Yiqi Zhang
abstract: Quasicrystals are ubiquitous in nature. They represent unique aperiodic materials featuring long-range order that occupy an intermediate niche between exactly periodic and disordered materials. These properties are reflected in the unusual evolutionary dynamics of excitations and unique localization properties of linear eigenmodes supported by quasicrystals. In particular, being the structures characterized by discrete rotational symmetry of order , photonic quasicrystals can support the stable propagation of linear vortex-carrying light beams and vortex solitons. However, the impact of discrete rotational symmetry of quasicrystals on the properties of vortex light states has not been investigated so far, as only the systems constructed using the simplest Penrose tiling or corresponding optically induced Penrose lattices are considered in this context. Here, we propose a broad class of quasicrystals with global topological defects—disclinations—introduced into their structure that allows to produce novel quasicrystalline structures with any desired order of discrete rotational symmetry from the basic Penrose structure. Such global topological deformation substantially enriches the linear spectrum of quasicrystals, allowing them to support new types of linear vortex states and bifurcating from them families of stable thresholdless vortex solitons with unusual intensity and phase distributions. We find two different classes of stable vortex solitons comprising in-phase or out-of-phase pairs of closely located bright spots, with total intensity distribution reflecting a particular discrete rotational symmetry of the quasicrystal with disclination. Remarkably, even low-charge vortex solitons can be stable in quasicrystals with disclinations, whereas stability intervals for them broaden with the decrease of the discrete rotational symmetry of quasicrystals. Our results extend the theory of localization in quasicrystals to structures with global topological deformation, highlighting emerging prospects for the robust transmission of power or information arising in these systems.
tldr: This paper studies vortex solitons in photonic quasicrystals with disclinations, focusing on their stability and intensity distributions.
motivation: To understand how global topological defects (disclinations) in quasicrystals affect the properties of vortex light states, which have not been investigated before.
method: The authors propose a class of quasicrystals with disclinations, analyze their linear spectrum, and numerically find families of stable vortex solitons.
result: Two classes of stable vortex solitons are found, with stability intervals broadening as discrete rotational symmetry decreases.
conclusion: The results extend localization theory to quasicrystals with topological deformations, suggesting potential for robust transmission of power or information.

title: Charting Light Harvesting In Purple Bacteria In Vivo
authors: Romain Rouxeljulian Lüttigmichael R. Jonesdonatas Zigmantasahttps://ror.org/012a77v79division Of Chemical Physics, Department Of Chemistry, Lund University, Lund Se-221 00, Swedenbhttps://ror.org/03c4mmv16department Of Physics, University Of Ottawa, Ottawa, ON K1N 6N5, Canadachttps://ror.org/0524sp257school Of Biochemistry, Biomedical Sciences Building, University Of Bristol, Bristol BS8 1TD, United Kingdom
abstract:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Volume 123, Issue 27, July 2026.
SignificanceTwo-dimensional electronic spectroscopy emerged as the method of choice to unravel molecular couplings and energy transfer pathways in photosynthetic systems. Experiments on individual photosynthetic complexes have been very successful, but ...
tldr: This paper uses two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy to study energy transfer in purple bacteria, focusing on molecular couplings and pathways in photosynthesis.
motivation: Understanding energy transfer in photosynthetic systems is important for biology and potentially for bio-inspired technologies, but the paper does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: Two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy experiments on photosynthetic complexes.
result: The study maps energy transfer pathways and molecular couplings in purple bacteria.
conclusion: The findings advance the understanding of natural light harvesting but have no direct relevance to quantum information theory or thermodynamics.

title: Density Evolution At Fluid-fluid Interfaces: A Generalized Gibbs-Duhem Theory
authors: Fei Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.11988v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The classical Gibbs-Duhem relation applies to quasi-static processes and neglects kinetic effects, leaving a fundamental gap between Gibbs thermodynamics and Newtonian mechanics. Here, we derive a generalized Gibbs-Duhem framework that incorporates kinetic contributions, thereby establishing a unified connection between classical thermodynamics and Newtonian mechanics. Based on this framework, we propose an alternative evolution equation governing density dynamics at fluid-fluid interfaces. In appropriate limiting cases, the resulting density evolution equation naturally recovers the definition of the speed of sound, Bernoulli's law, and the van der Waals equation of state (EOS).
tldr: This paper derives a generalized Gibbs-Duhem framework incorporating kinetic contributions to model density evolution at fluid-fluid interfaces.
motivation: The classical Gibbs-Duhem relation neglects kinetic effects, leaving a gap between thermodynamics and Newtonian mechanics; the authors aim to unify them.
method: The authors derive a generalized Gibbs-Duhem equation that includes kinetic terms and propose an alternative evolution equation for density at fluid-fluid interfaces.
result: The resulting density evolution equation recovers the speed of sound, Bernoulli's law, and the van der Waals equation of state in appropriate limits.
conclusion: The framework bridges classical thermodynamics and Newtonian mechanics for fluid interfaces, but has no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Bulk And Microphase Separation In Chiral Active Systems
authors: Sumeja Burekovi\'c, S. J. Kole, Ananyo Maitra, Cesare Nardini
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12045v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many active particles phase-separate due to quorum-sensing interactions, and their self-propulsion mechanisms often break chiral symmetry. Using particle and continuum models, we uncover the role of chirality in inducing bulk or microphase separation, including a chiral phase formed of vapor bubbles. Analytical predictions for the emergence of these phases require a coarse-graining technique based on multiple-scale analysis. Further, introducing a minimal active field theory, we show that, in the bulk phase separation regime, chirality does not alter the diffusive [MATH] coarsening law nor the dynamical exponent associated with capillary waves, but induces traveling waves at the interface. We finally demonstrate that, even in the absence of fluid flows, chirality can cause the breakup of elongated droplets, resembling phenomena previously observed experimentally.
tldr: This paper studies phase separation in chiral active systems, focusing on bulk and microphase separation induced by chirality.
motivation: Active particles often phase-separate due to quorum-sensing interactions, and many self-propulsion mechanisms break chiral symmetry, motivating the study of chirality's role in phase separation.
method: The authors use particle and continuum models, along with a coarse-graining technique based on multiple-scale analysis, and introduce a minimal active field theory.
result: Chirality induces bulk or microphase separation, including a chiral phase of vapor bubbles; it does not alter the diffusive coarsening law but induces traveling waves at the interface and can cause breakup of elongated droplets.
conclusion: Chirality significantly influences phase separation morphology in active systems, with potential experimental relevance.

title: Wichmann-Kroll Correction To The Interelectronic Interaction In He- And Li-Like Ions
authors: J. Sommerfeldt, V. A. Yerokhin, Z. Harman, C. H. Keitel
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12168v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a theoretical study of the higher-order QED contribution to the interelectronic interaction in He- and Li-like ions, where a virtual electron-positron loop is inserted into the photon line of the one-photon exchange diagram. Our approach is based on the Dirac-Coulomb Green's function and accounts for the interaction of the virtual [MATH] pair with the electric field of the nucleus to all orders in [MATH], with [MATH] being the fine-structure constant and [MATH] the atomic charge number. We show that the numerical convergence of the involved integrals can be significantly improved by explicitly subtracting the non-gauge-invariant spurious contributions from the integrands. We present improved numerical values for this contribution to the Lamb shift over a wide range of nuclear charge numbers [MATH]. Our calculations agree well with previous results by Artemyev and co-workers~[Phys. Rev. A , 3529 (1997); Phys. Rev. A , 45 (1999)] for He-like ions, but we find a discrepancy in the Li-like case. Moreover, we calculate the finite nuclear size correction to this diagram, which can reduce its size by more than 5\% for heavy ions. The improved QED calculations not only decrease the uncertainty of theoretical predictions for the interelectronic interaction in few-electron ions but the methods could also be used in the future to improve calculations of closely related one-electron two-loop QED diagrams.
tldr: This paper presents high-precision QED calculations of the Wichmann-Kroll correction to interelectronic interactions in He- and Li-like ions.
motivation: Accurate theoretical predictions for few-electron ions are needed to interpret spectroscopic experiments and test QED in strong fields.
method: The authors use the Dirac-Coulomb Green's function to compute the one-photon exchange diagram with a virtual electron-positron loop, subtracting spurious non-gauge-invariant contributions to improve convergence.
result: Improved numerical values for the Wichmann-Kroll contribution to the Lamb shift are obtained for a wide range of nuclear charges, with a discrepancy found for Li-like ions compared to previous work.
conclusion: The calculations reduce theoretical uncertainties and can be extended to related two-loop QED diagrams.

title: Peak-Decomposition-Free Inverse Metrology Of Hyperspectral Moir\'e Photoluminescence
authors: Katsunori Wakabayashi
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12325v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hyperspectral photoluminescence (PL) of moir\'e transition-metal dichalcogenide heterobilayers encodes spatially varying exciton landscapes, but extracting that information is hampered by the ambiguity of multi-peak spectral decomposition. Here we develop a peak-decomposition-free inverse framework for quantitative optical metrology of effective disorder coordinates. From the raw cube [MATH] we construct physically motivated descriptor maps -- centroid energy, dominant emission energy, spectral width, low/high spectral-weight ratio, and dominant--centroid offset. Their spatial autocorrelation hierarchy and covariance structure form a robust descriptor fingerprint of multi-scale disorder-sensitive spectral statistics. By matching these descriptor summary statistics to a minimal smooth-plus-trap generative model through a grid-Bayesian inverse, we infer effective disorder coordinates [MATH] with explicit uncertainties. Using synthetic PL cubes generated from controlled multi-scale landscapes, we recover the well-identified smooth-disorder coordinates and constrain the trap sector up to a strength--density degeneracy. We report this degeneracy explicitly as an intrinsic identifiability limit rather than a deficiency of the method, and map four canonical disorder regimes onto a disorder-coordinate diagram. The descriptor statistics are stable against shot noise and pixel pitch, and behave predictably under optical-resolution and energy-window changes. The same pipeline ingests experimental cubes without modification, making it directly applicable to two-dimensional and moir\'e materials. Our results establish descriptor-based hyperspectral PL as a practical, minimal-assumption route to optical disorder diagnostics and provide the validated core of a reusable analysis workflow () for moir\'e exciton systems.
tldr: This paper develops a peak-decomposition-free inverse metrology framework for hyperspectral photoluminescence of moiré TMD heterobilayers to infer disorder coordinates.
motivation: Extracting spatially varying exciton landscapes from hyperspectral PL is hampered by the ambiguity of multi-peak spectral decomposition.
method: The authors construct physically motivated descriptor maps from raw spectral cubes and match their summary statistics to a generative model via grid-Bayesian inversion.
result: The method recovers smooth-disorder coordinates and identifies a strength-density degeneracy in the trap sector, mapping four disorder regimes onto a coordinate diagram.
conclusion: Descriptor-based hyperspectral PL provides a practical, minimal-assumption route to optical disorder diagnostics for moiré exciton systems.

title: Cyclic Codes Over A Commutative Non-unitary Ring Of Order 4
authors: Jon-Lark Kim Marvin Olavides
abstract: ArXiv:2607.11965v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be the commutative non-unitary ring of order [MATH] arising in the classification of Fine. In this paper, we investigate cyclic codes over [MATH] through their associated residue and torsion codes over [MATH]. We introduce the notions of twisted and untwisted cyclic codes and characterize cyclicity in terms of a compatibility condition involving the twist map and the cyclic shift. Connections between cyclic codes over [MATH] and binary quasi-cyclic codes are established via Gray maps. In particular, we show that the Gray image of a cyclic code over [MATH] is a binary quasi-cyclic code of index [MATH]. We also study duality properties of cyclic codes over [MATH] and prove that the dual of a cyclic code is again cyclic. Finally, we classify permutation inequivalent cyclic codes over [MATH] for lengths [MATH] and determine various structural properties of these codes.
tldr: This paper studies cyclic codes over a commutative non-unitary ring of order 4, focusing on algebraic coding theory without quantum information or thermodynamics connections.
motivation: To understand the structure and properties of cyclic codes over a specific non-unitary ring, extending classical coding theory.
method: The authors define twisted and untwisted cyclic codes, characterize cyclicity via a compatibility condition, and use Gray maps to relate codes over the ring to binary quasi-cyclic codes.
result: They establish that the Gray image of a cyclic code over the ring is a binary quasi-cyclic code, prove duality properties, and classify permutation inequivalent cyclic codes for small lengths.
conclusion: The work contributes to algebraic coding theory but does not address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: The Certification Limits Of KS-Type Layer Relaxations: A Square-Root Ceiling And Its Breakdown
authors: Guillaume Lecomte
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12134v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A separable bilinear layer relaxation assigns a population cost to each layer and a nonpositive bilinear coupling to each pair of layers, then excludes a profile span whenever the relaxed minimum exceeds a reference value. We ask what a Kuznetsov-Sahinidis-type relaxation can certify at best. Let gamma = g(1) be the singleton-layer cost. For every valid relaxation with gamma > -1/2, every reference bounded per particle, and every underlying system satisfying two elementary low-energy witness conditions, we prove that the certified deficit N - rho(N) is at most of order sqrt(N), with an explicit bound depending only on the reference bound and gamma. Thus no relaxation in this class can certify a larger asymptotic deficit, independently of the detailed layer cost, interaction kernel, or reference. The threshold is sharp in the abstract witness class: at gamma = -1/2 we construct a valid relaxation with a bounded sound reference and deficit N - 1. The geometric Lennard-Jones system behaves differently. A three-atom chain restores the square-root ceiling at the endpoint, while sufficiently negative singleton costs allow valid relaxations with linear deficit. For still lower costs, beyond the stability constant, no sound relaxation excludes any span. These regimes define a certification spectrum for layer relaxations and reveal a reentrant transition between no exclusion, linear exclusion, and the universal square-root ceiling.
tldr: This paper studies certification limits of a specific class of layer relaxations, proving a square-root ceiling on the certified deficit and showing exceptions for certain systems.
motivation: To understand the fundamental limitations of Kuznetsov-Sahinidis-type layer relaxations in certifying properties of complex systems.
method: The author defines a class of separable bilinear layer relaxations and proves upper bounds on the certified deficit using low-energy witness conditions, then constructs counterexamples for specific parameter regimes.
result: For valid relaxations with singleton-layer cost gamma > -1/2, the certified deficit is at most O(sqrt(N)), with a sharp threshold at gamma = -1/2 where linear deficit becomes possible, and a reentrant transition in the Lennard-Jones system.
conclusion: The certification power of these relaxations is fundamentally limited by a square-root ceiling, except in special cases where linear exclusion or no exclusion occurs.

title: Generalized Segmented Grand For Guesswork Reduction In Turbo Product Decoding
authors: Lukas Rapp, Jiewei Feng, Muriel M\'edard, Ken R. Duffy
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12147v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Guessing random additive noise decoding (GRAND) can efficiently decode any moderately redundant code with near maximum likelihood (ML) performance via noise effect guessing. For binary linear codes, Rowshan and Yuan's Segmented GRAND was the first to show that constrained guessing can reduce guesswork. Although powerful, their approach requires a specific parity-check matrix structure that limits the number of constraints that can be exploited as well as the class of applicable codes. Here we introduce GSegGRAND, a generalization of Segmented GRAND that circumvents its limitations. Built on a novel parity check structure and a transformation that maps codes into this structure, GSegGRAND efficiently incorporates up to log2(n) constraints for a wide range of codes, reducing guesswork by an additional 75% over Segmented GRAND. To leverage that advantage for soft-output decoding, we derive an accurate soft-output (SO) equation for GSegGRAND by extending soft-output GRAND (SOGRAND) to incorporate constrained guessing. Applying this SO to turbo product decoding, GSegGRAND achieves up to 88% guesswork reduction, making it a promising candidate for low-latency decoding in future communication systems.
tldr: This paper presents a generalized segmented GRAND decoding algorithm that reduces guesswork for turbo product decoding.
motivation: Existing segmented GRAND has limitations in the number of constraints and applicable code classes, motivating a more general approach.
method: The authors introduce a novel parity check structure and a transformation to map codes into this structure, enabling up to log2(n) constraints, and derive a soft-output equation for constrained guessing.
result: GSegGRAND achieves up to 75% additional guesswork reduction over Segmented GRAND, and up to 88% reduction in turbo product decoding.
conclusion: GSegGRAND is a promising low-latency decoding candidate for future communication systems.

title: Residual-Certified Adaptive Tracking Of Solution Manifolds In Parametric Dynamical Systems
authors: Yiran Xing, Yuandi Xu, Sulei Hu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.12351v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents a residual-certified adaptive method for tracking local solution manifolds in parametric dynamical systems. The method combines local POD reduction, full physical residual checks, state-distance snapshot forgetting, high-fidelity resampling, and a lightweight physics-informed neural correction. Instead of learning one global parameter-to-state map, the algorithm maintains the currently active local branch and updates it when the residual indicates loss of validity. The analysis explains why residual thresholds are meaningful on regular branches through local residual-error control, and why stricter local updates are needed near folds or other degenerate neighborhoods. Numerical studies on Ostwald ripening, a particle population-balance model, and the Bratu equation test the approach across low-dimensional dynamics, nonlinear nonlocal residual compensation, and near-fold model failure. The results show that residual-certified local model management can concentrate high-fidelity computation in difficult parameter regions while preserving an interpretable link between surrogate prediction, physical consistency, and active-branch tracking.
tldr: A residual-certified adaptive method for tracking solution manifolds in parametric dynamical systems using POD reduction and neural correction.
motivation: To efficiently track solution manifolds in parametric dynamical systems by adaptively updating local reduced-order models based on residual checks.
method: Combines local POD reduction, full physical residual checks, state-distance snapshot forgetting, high-fidelity resampling, and a lightweight physics-informed neural correction.
result: Demonstrates that residual-certified local model management concentrates high-fidelity computation in difficult parameter regions while preserving interpretability.
conclusion: The method provides an interpretable link between surrogate prediction, physical consistency, and active-branch tracking for parametric dynamical systems.
